title: Argument Evaluation Without Ground Truth
position: Philosophical inquiry can progress even when no decisive answer is available. Evaluators may disagree about a conclusion while still converging on whether a particular objection is relevant, logically coherent, and damaging to the stated position. Therefore, training people or systems to assess contextualized arguments is a legitimate route to better judgment on conceptual questions.

title: Intuitions as Prima Facie Evidence
position: Many philosophical disputes concern concepts that competent speakers already possess, such as knowledge, freedom, and fairness. Carefully elicited intuitions about cases therefore provide prima facie evidence about how those concepts apply. Such evidence is defeasible, but abandoning it entirely would remove one of the few direct sources of information available in conceptual inquiry.

title: Reflective Equilibrium as Philosophical Method
position: A defensible philosophical view should emerge from mutual adjustment among particular judgments, general principles, and relevant background theories. Reflective equilibrium improves on rigid foundationalism because no single class of commitments is immune from revision. Coherence reached through wide and informed revision is therefore a strong indicator of rational acceptability.

title: Experimental Philosophy as a Corrective
position: Traditional philosophers often generalize from their own reactions to thought experiments. Experimental philosophy improves the evidential basis of such claims by measuring how judgments vary across populations, framings, and demographic groups. Where intuitions are unstable or culturally parochial, their authority in philosophical argument should be correspondingly reduced.

title: Philosophical Expertise Deserves Deference
position: Professional philosophers spend years learning distinctions, objections, and dialectical history that non-specialists usually lack. Although expertise does not settle philosophical questions, persistent expert consensus should rationally influence a layperson’s credence, just as informed judgment matters in other complex fields. Refusing all deference would ignore substantial evidence about comparative competence.

title: Deep Philosophical Disagreement Favors Suspension
position: When informed and intellectually responsible peers examine the same philosophical issue yet reach opposing conclusions, each gains evidence that their own reasoning may be mistaken. In domains lacking decisive external checks, this higher-order evidence is especially important. Therefore, persistent peer disagreement often makes substantial reduction of confidence, and sometimes suspension of judgment, rationally appropriate.

title: Conceptual Engineering Over Conceptual Analysis
position: Philosophers should not merely discover how inherited concepts happen to function. When a concept is confused, exclusionary, or poorly suited to inquiry, we should redesign it to serve clearer epistemic and social purposes. Conceptual engineering is therefore often more valuable than attempting to preserve ordinary usage.

title: Methodological Naturalism in Philosophy
position: Philosophical claims about mind, knowledge, agency, and value should be continuous with our best empirical theories. When an armchair argument conflicts with well-supported science, the philosophical premise should normally yield. Methodological naturalism disciplines speculation by requiring philosophical accounts to fit the world revealed through successful inquiry.

title: Formal Models Clarify Philosophical Disputes
position: Many philosophical disagreements persist because key assumptions remain implicit. Formal models force theorists to specify variables, inferential relations, and trade-offs, making hidden commitments visible. Even when a model idealizes heavily, the resulting precision often advances debate by revealing exactly where parties disagree.

title: Philosophy as Therapeutic Dissolution
position: Many traditional philosophical problems arise because language is detached from the practical contexts that give expressions their use. Rather than constructing theories about artificial puzzles, philosophers should diagnose the linguistic temptation that generates them. Once the misuse is exposed, the apparent problem may dissolve instead of being solved.

title: Knowledge Requires Safety from Error
position: A true belief does not amount to knowledge when it is true merely by luck. To exclude lucky success, knowledge requires safety: in nearby possible situations where the subject forms the belief in the same way, the belief would not easily have been false. This modal condition explains why ordinary perception can yield knowledge while classic Gettier cases do not.

title: Reliabilism About Justification
position: A belief is epistemically justified when it is produced by a process that tends to generate true rather than false beliefs in the relevant range of cases. This explains why perception and memory can justify without requiring subjects to possess arguments for their reliability. Justification is fundamentally a matter of objective truth-conduciveness, not reflective access.

title: Internal Access Is Necessary for Justification
position: Epistemic justification concerns whether a believer has conducted inquiry responsibly from their own point of view. Therefore, all factors that determine whether a belief is justified must be accessible through reflection, at least in principle. External facts unknown to the subject may affect whether the belief is true, but not whether holding it is rational.

title: Default Entitlement to Testimony
position: Human knowledge depends extensively on what others tell us, and requiring independent evidence for every speaker would make learning impossible. Hearers are therefore prima facie entitled to accept sincere-seeming testimony unless they possess specific defeaters. Testimony is a basic source of justification rather than merely an inferential shortcut from prior evidence about reliability.

title: Knowledge Is Closed Under Known Implication
position: If a person knows a proposition and competently recognizes that it entails another proposition, then after deducing the consequence they know that consequence as well. Denying closure makes knowledge irrationally fragmentary: one could know premises while failing to know an obvious implication explicitly derived from them. Closure is thus a constitutive norm of epistemic consistency.

title: Contextualism About Knowledge Ascriptions
position: The truth conditions of sentences attributing knowledge vary with conversational context. In ordinary settings, relevant alternatives are limited, so “Mira knows the bank is open” may be true; in a skeptical discussion, stricter alternatives become salient and the same sentence may be false. Contextualism preserves both ordinary knowledge claims and the force of skeptical reasoning.

title: Practical Stakes Affect Knowledge
position: Whether evidence is sufficient for knowledge can depend on what is practically at stake. A traveler may know that the train stops in Dover when little depends on it, yet fail to know the same proposition when missing the stop would be catastrophic and checking is easy. High stakes make previously ignored possibilities epistemically relevant.

title: Epistemic Permissivism
position: A body of evidence need not determine a unique rational attitude. When evidence is complex and competing explanatory virtues are difficult to compare, multiple doxastic responses may be reasonable for agents who weight considerations differently. Epistemic permissivism better reflects rational pluralism than a rigid uniqueness thesis.

title: Virtue Epistemology and Credit for Truth
position: Knowledge is not merely true belief produced by a reliable process; the truth must be attributable to the believer’s intellectual competence. This credit condition explains why lucky true beliefs and truths delivered by a malfunctioning environment fail to be knowledge. Knowing is a kind of successful cognitive performance because of ability.

title: Ordinary Knowledge Survives Skeptical Hypotheses
position: A remote skeptical scenario, such as systematic deception, does not defeat ordinary knowledge merely because one cannot conclusively rule it out. Knowledge requires reasonable discrimination among relevant alternatives, not certainty against every logically possible error. Since skeptical hypotheses are unsupported and explanatorily idle, they are not normally relevant alternatives.

title: Falsifiability as a Demarcation Criterion
position: A theory counts as genuinely scientific only if it exposes itself to possible empirical refutation. Predictions that could conflict with observation distinguish risky inquiry from systems that reinterpret every outcome as confirmation. Falsifiability therefore provides the clearest boundary between science and pseudoscience.

title: Inference to the Best Explanation
position: When several hypotheses fit the available evidence, rational inquiry should prefer the one that would, if true, best explain that evidence. Explanatory virtues such as simplicity, coherence, and unification are not merely aesthetic; they indicate which hypothesis is most likely to be true. Much successful science relies on this abductive form of reasoning.

title: Scientific Realism from Novel Success
position: Mature scientific theories often predict phenomena that were not used in their construction. It would be an extraordinary coincidence if theories achieved such novel success while being radically wrong about the unobservable entities and structures they posit. The best explanation of sustained predictive success is that central theoretical claims are at least approximately true.

title: Constructive Empiricism
position: The aim of science is not to deliver literally true accounts of unobservable reality but to produce theories that are empirically adequate: true about observable phenomena. Accepting a theory requires believing what it says about observables while merely using its claims about hidden entities. This stance respects scientific practice without exceeding the evidence.

title: Underdetermination Limits Theoretical Belief
position: For any finite body of observations, multiple incompatible theories can often be constructed that fit the data equally well. Since evidence alone cannot select uniquely among empirically equivalent rivals, confidence in a particular theoretical ontology should remain modest. Scientific data warrant less metaphysical commitment than realists commonly assume.

title: Laws of Nature as the Best System
position: The laws of nature are the axioms and theorems of the deductive system that best balances simplicity, strength, and fit with the total history of events. This best-system account avoids mysterious governing necessities while explaining why laws summarize broad regularities. Lawhood is a feature of the optimal description of the world.

title: Interventionism About Causation
position: A variable X causes Y when suitably intervening to change X would change Y, holding relevant background factors fixed. This interventionist account connects causation to experimental practice and distinguishes genuine causes from mere correlations. Counterfactual manipulability therefore provides the most useful analysis of causal claims.

title: Social Values Inevitably Enter Science
position: Scientists must decide which questions to study, what error rates are tolerable, and when evidence is sufficient for public action. These choices have social consequences and cannot be fixed by data alone. Therefore, value-free science is impossible, and responsible inquiry should make its social and ethical values explicit rather than pretending neutrality.

title: Replication as the Core of Scientific Reliability
position: A finding should not be treated as established until independent researchers can reproduce it under sufficiently similar conditions. Replication filters out chance results, hidden analytic flexibility, and laboratory-specific artifacts. Scientific institutions should therefore prioritize repeated confirmation over the constant production of novel claims.

title: Unification as Scientific Understanding
position: A scientific explanation provides deeper understanding when it derives many apparently separate phenomena from a small set of principles. Unification reduces brute coincidence and reveals common structure behind diverse observations. Other things equal, a more unifying theory is therefore explanatorily superior.

title: Classical Logic as the Default Logic
position: Classical logic should remain the default framework for evaluating arguments because it is simple, mathematically powerful, and deeply integrated with successful reasoning in mathematics and science. Alternative logics are best understood as specialized tools for restricted purposes. Departures from classical consequence require a stronger justification than ordinary use of it.

title: The Principle of Explosion Is Valid
position: From a contradiction, any proposition follows in classical logic. This is not an arbitrary defect: if both P and not-P are accepted, disjunctive introduction and disjunctive syllogism yield any Q. Rejecting explosion therefore requires abandoning independently plausible inference rules, so rational theories should remain contradiction-free.

title: The Law of Excluded Middle Is Universally Valid
position: For every proposition P, either P or not-P. Denying excluded middle confuses our inability to determine a truth value with the proposition’s lacking one. Since reality is not made indeterminate by ignorance, excluded middle is a universally valid logical law.

title: Paraconsistent Logic for Inconsistent Theories
position: Some important bodies of information contain contradictions yet remain nontrivial. Paraconsistent logics preserve meaningful inference by blocking explosion, allowing reasoners to isolate conflicts without deriving everything. They are therefore better models of reasoning under inconsistency than classical logic.

title: Relevance Is Necessary for Valid Implication
position: An implication should not count as valid when its conclusion is wholly unrelated to its premises. Classical logic allows any truth to be inferred from an arbitrary premise and any conclusion from a contradiction, obscuring the inferential connection that argumentation requires. A genuine consequence relation must therefore impose a relevance constraint.

title: Formal Fallacies Are More Serious Than Informal Fallacies
position: A formal fallacy guarantees that the conclusion does not follow from the premises, whereas an informal fallacy often depends on context and can occur in arguments whose conclusions are nevertheless well supported. Because formal invalidity is objective and structurally decisive, detecting formal fallacies should take priority in argument evaluation.

title: The Burden of Proof Falls on Positive Claimants
position: A person asserting that something exists, occurred, or should be adopted bears the burden of providing reasons. Merely demanding that skeptics disprove the claim would license belief in indefinitely many unsupported possibilities. Rational debate therefore begins from withholding acceptance until positive support is supplied.

title: The Principle of Charity in Interpretation
position: When a text or speaker admits several plausible interpretations, interpreters should prefer the version that is most coherent and rational. Charity prevents superficial refutations based on slips, ambiguity, or unrepresentative formulations. It is therefore a necessary norm for fair argument assessment.

title: Argument Maps Improve Reasoning
position: Representing arguments as explicit networks of claims, supports, and objections reduces cognitive load and reveals hidden dependencies. Argument maps make it easier to identify unsupported premises, duplicated reasons, and points of genuine disagreement. Their systematic use should therefore improve philosophical deliberation.

title: Dialectical Success Is Evidence of Argument Quality
position: An argument that survives sustained criticism from informed opponents has passed a demanding test. Dialectical resilience exposes hidden assumptions and forces clarification in ways solitary reflection cannot. Therefore, durability across adversarial exchange is significant evidence that an argument is strong.

title: Descriptivism About Proper Names
position: A proper name refers through a cluster of descriptions associated with it by competent speakers. The name “Aristotle,” for example, picks out whoever best satisfies central descriptions such as being Plato’s student and Alexander’s tutor. Descriptivism explains both how names acquire cognitive significance and how speakers identify their referents.

title: The Causal-Historical Theory of Names
position: A name refers to an individual because present uses belong to a causal chain originating in an initial naming event. Speakers need not possess uniquely identifying descriptions; they need only intend to use the name as members of the linguistic community do. This explains successful reference despite ignorance and error.

title: Semantic Externalism
position: The contents of at least some thoughts and words depend partly on the speaker’s environment. Two internally identical people can mean different substances by “water” if their communities interact with different underlying liquids. Meaning is therefore not wholly fixed by what is in the speaker’s head.

title: Meaning Is Use
position: The meaning of an expression is constituted by its role in human practices rather than by an abstract object paired with the word. To understand a term is to know how it is appropriately used across language games. Philosophical confusion often arises when words are detached from those rules of use.

title: Truth-Conditional Semantics Is Fundamental
position: To know the meaning of a declarative sentence is, centrally, to know the conditions under which it would be true. Truth conditions explain compositionality, entailment, and disagreement by locating sentences within a structured representation of possible states of affairs. Other pragmatic effects can be added after literal content is fixed.

title: Conversational Implicature Preserves Minimal Semantics
position: Many apparently context-sensitive aspects of communication are pragmatic implicatures generated by cooperative reasoning, not parts of literal meaning. A speaker who says “some students passed” usually suggests that not all passed, though the sentence remains literally compatible with all passing. Separating semantics from implicature preserves a stable, compositional core.

title: Speaker Meaning Is Intention-Based
position: What a speaker means on an occasion is determined by an intention that the audience recognize that very intention and respond partly because of that recognition. This reflexive structure distinguishes communication from merely causing a reaction. Meaning is grounded in overtly audience-directed intentions.

title: Supervaluationism About Vagueness
position: Vague language admits multiple admissible precise interpretations. A statement is supertrue when it is true on all admissible precisifications and superfalse when false on all; borderline statements may be neither. This account preserves classical logic for determinately true claims while explaining indeterminate cases.

title: Metaphor Expresses Propositional Content
position: A successful metaphor communicates a proposition beyond the literal meaning of its words. Saying “the city is asleep” can convey that activity is unusually low and responsiveness is diminished. Metaphorical interpretation is therefore a context-guided way of arriving at nonliteral truth-conditional content.

title: Inferentialism About Conceptual Content
position: The content of a concept is constituted by the inferences a competent user is entitled and committed to make with it. Understanding “and,” “cause,” or “rights” consists in grasping their roles in reasoning rather than associating them with private images. Inferential role explains why meaning is normative and publicly assessable.

title: Presentism About Time
position: Only present events and objects exist. The past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the apparent passage of time reflects reality’s continual renewal rather than our perspective on a static block. Presentism best captures the asymmetry between what is actual now and what merely was or will be.

title: Eternalism and the Block Universe
position: Past, present, and future events all equally exist within a four-dimensional spacetime. The privileged “now” is perspectival, like “here,” and temporal passage is a feature of consciousness rather than a change in what exists. Eternalism fits naturally with relativity and gives straightforward truthmakers for claims about every time.

title: Perdurantism About Persistence
position: Objects persist by having different temporal parts at different times, just as a road extends through different spatial segments. Change is then the possession of incompatible properties by distinct temporal parts rather than by one wholly present object. Perdurantism offers a clean account of persistence through radical change.

title: Realism About Universals
position: Distinct objects can genuinely share one property, such as redness or mass, and this commonality grounds resemblance and general laws. Universals—repeatable entities instantiated in many places—provide the most direct explanation of such shared structure. Nominalist paraphrases describe patterns without explaining what makes them patterns of the same kind.

title: Nominalism About Properties
position: Only particular things exist; talk of properties and universals is a useful way of grouping resembling particulars. We do not need a single entity called redness present in every red object. Nominalism respects ontological economy while preserving all ordinary and scientific descriptions through predicates, classes, or resemblance relations.

title: Metaphysical Grounding Is Indispensable
position: Some facts obtain in virtue of more fundamental facts: a set exists because its members do, and a social institution exists because people and practices sustain it. This asymmetric dependence is not captured by causation, entailment, or mere supervenience. Grounding is therefore an indispensable primitive for articulating metaphysical structure.

title: Unrestricted Mereological Composition
position: Whenever there are some objects, there is a further object composed of exactly them. Restricting composition to tables, organisms, or other familiar wholes requires a vague and arbitrary boundary. Unrestricted composition offers a simple, precise ontology and allows ordinary objects to be treated as special cases among many fusions.

title: Mereological Nihilism
position: Strictly speaking, there are no composite objects; only fundamental simples arranged table-wise, organism-wise, and so on. This view avoids puzzles about vague boundaries, coincident objects, and arbitrary fusions. Ordinary talk remains useful and can be paraphrased without committing us to wholes.

title: Modal Realism About Possible Worlds
position: Possible worlds are concrete realities as complete as our own, and “possibly P” means that P is true at some such world. This analysis reduces modality to quantification over nonmodal entities and gives a uniform semantics for counterfactuals, necessity, and possibility. The abundance of worlds is a fair price for theoretical unity.

title: Dispositional Essentialism
position: Natural properties are essentially tied to the causal powers they confer. A property that behaved entirely differently would not be the same property in another world. This view explains laws as arising from the natures of properties rather than as external regularities imposed on an otherwise passive mosaic.

title: Physicalism from Causal Closure
position: Every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause. Mental events plainly influence bodily behavior, so either they are physical or their effects are systematically overdetermined by independent physical causes. Because pervasive overdetermination is implausible, mental events are physical.

title: Conceivability Supports Property Dualism
position: We can coherently conceive of a physical duplicate of a human being that lacks conscious experience. If such a zombie is genuinely conceivable, it is metaphysically possible; and if it is possible, physical facts do not necessitate phenomenal facts. Consciousness therefore involves properties beyond the physical.

title: Functionalism About Mental States
position: A mental state is defined by its causal role: the inputs that tend to produce it, its relations to other internal states, and the behavior it tends to cause. Pain, for example, is whatever state mediates injury, distress, avoidance, and characteristic reasoning. Functionalism explains how diverse physical systems could share a mind.

title: Mind-Brain Identity Theory
position: Mental states are identical with neural states, just as lightning is identical with electrical discharge. Correlations between experience and brain activity are best explained by identity rather than by two coordinated phenomena. A mature neuroscience will discover which neural processes particular experiences are.

title: The Computational Theory of Mind
position: Cognition is computation over internal representations. Perception supplies representational inputs, cognitive processes transform them according to algorithms, and action results from computed outputs. This framework explains systematic reasoning and supports implementation across biological and artificial hardware.

title: Higher-Order Thought Theory of Consciousness
position: A mental state becomes conscious when the subject has a suitable higher-order representation of being in that state. Unconscious perception can guide behavior, but awareness arises when the system represents its own first-order state. This explains the difference between information processing and conscious access.

title: Global Workspace Theory of Conscious Access
position: Information becomes conscious when it is globally broadcast to multiple cognitive systems, including memory, planning, language, and action control. Local unconscious processors remain modular, while a global workspace makes selected content widely available. Consciousness is thus the functional availability of information across the mind.

title: Representationalism About Experience
position: The phenomenal character of an experience is determined by what the experience represents. A red experience feels the way it does because it presents the world as containing a certain color property. This explains the transparency of experience: introspection seems directed outward to represented features, not inward to mental paint.

title: Illusionism About Phenomenal Properties
position: People are conscious, but introspection misrepresents their mental states as possessing intrinsic, ineffable qualitative properties. What needs explanation is not mysterious qualia but why cognitive systems judge and report that such qualia exist. Illusionism preserves the functional and behavioral facts while avoiding an ontologically intractable residue.

title: The Extended Mind
position: Cognitive processes can extend beyond the skull when external resources are reliably integrated into problem solving. A notebook that a person automatically consults may play the same functional role as biological memory. If internal and external components are equivalently available and trusted, both can be parts of one cognitive system.

title: Psychological Continuity Grounds Personal Identity
position: A person persists through time when later mental life is appropriately continuous with earlier mental life through memory, intention, character, and other psychological connections. Bodily replacement would not destroy the person if this continuity remained. What matters for being the same person is the continuation of a mind, not the persistence of particular matter.

title: Bodily Continuity Grounds Personal Identity
position: A person is the same individual over time when the same living human body continues through ordinary biological processes. Memories and character can change radically without creating a new person, while a perfect psychological copy in another body would remain a copy. Bodily continuity best matches legal, interpersonal, and biological practices of reidentification.

title: Animalism About Persons
position: Each of us is fundamentally a human animal, an organism that begins before sophisticated consciousness and may survive its loss. Thinking is something the animal does, not evidence for a separate person constituted by psychological relations. Animalism offers a unified account of prenatal existence, ordinary life, and persistence in severe cognitive decline.

title: The Brain Criterion of Identity
position: A person follows the continued functioning brain, or the parts of it that sustain consciousness and memory. The brain integrates bodily information, carries learned dispositions, and generates the stream of experience. In transplant cases, it is therefore more plausible that the person goes with the brain than with the remainder of the body.

title: Narrative Identity
position: Personal identity is partly constituted by the evolving story through which a person organizes memories, values, relationships, and future projects. A coherent self-narrative makes experiences intelligible as belonging to one life and supports responsibility and agency. Identity is therefore not merely biological continuity but an interpretive achievement.

title: Reductionism About Personal Identity
position: There is no further fact about personal identity beyond physical and psychological continuity relations. Once all facts about brains, bodies, memories, intentions, and causal connections are fixed, asking whether the “same self” remains adds no additional question. Personal identity is reducible to these more basic relations.

title: Non-Branching Psychological Continuity
position: Psychological continuity is sufficient for identity only when it does not branch. A later person is identical to an earlier one if they uniquely continue the earlier psychology; when two equal continuers exist, neither is strictly identical. The non-branching clause preserves the logic of identity while retaining the importance of psychological relations.

title: Memory as the Criterion of Personal Identity
position: A later person is the same as an earlier person when the later person can genuinely remember the earlier person’s experiences. Memory connects consciousness across time and grounds responsibility for past action. Where first-person memory is preserved, personal identity is preserved.

title: A Simple Soul Grounds Personal Identity
position: Personal identity through radical bodily and psychological change is best explained by the persistence of an immaterial subject of experience. A simple soul is not divisible into temporal or spatial parts, so it can remain numerically identical while its mental states change. This provides a determinate bearer of consciousness across time.

title: Identity Is Not What Matters in Survival
position: What rationally matters in survival is psychological continuity and connectedness, not strict numerical identity. In a perfect duplication case, identity may be indeterminate or absent, yet each successor can preserve the original’s memories, projects, and relationships. Prudential concern should track these continuities rather than an all-or-nothing metaphysical fact.

title: Libertarian Agent Causation
position: A free action cannot be wholly determined by prior events, yet mere randomness would not give the agent control. The best account is that persons themselves can initiate causal chains without being determined to do so by earlier states. Agent causation makes the individual, rather than an event inside them, the ultimate source of action.

title: Reasons-Responsive Compatibilism
position: A person acts freely when their action issues from a mechanism that can recognize and respond appropriately to reasons across a suitable range of circumstances. Determinism does not remove this capacity; it explains why the mechanism responds as it does. Freedom is rational self-governance, not metaphysical exemption from causation.

title: The Consequence Argument for Incompatibilism
position: If determinism is true, every present action follows from the laws of nature and facts about the remote past. No one has control over those laws or past facts, and no one has control over the consequences of things over which they have no control. Therefore, no one has control over present actions under determinism.

title: Frankfurt Cases Refute Alternative Possibilities
position: A person can be morally responsible even when they could not have acted otherwise. Suppose a hidden controller would force the agent to choose wrongly if they began to choose well, but the agent independently chooses wrongly and the controller never intervenes. Responsibility appears intact despite the absence of an alternative possibility.

title: The Manipulation Argument Against Compatibilism
position: If neuroscientists covertly program a person’s values so that they rationally choose a crime, the person seems unfree even if their deliberation is reasons-responsive. A deterministically developed ordinary agent differs only in the history and complexity of the causal process. Therefore, standard compatibilist conditions fail to distinguish manipulation from ordinary determination.

title: Hard Incompatibilism
position: Whether actions are determined or indeterministic, no one possesses the kind of ultimate control required for basic-desert moral responsibility. Determinism traces action to factors beyond the agent, while indeterminism adds luck rather than authorship. We should therefore reject retributive blame while retaining forward-looking practices of protection, rehabilitation, and moral influence.

title: Sourcehood Is More Important Than Alternatives
position: Freedom depends primarily on whether an action flows from the agent’s own values, judgments, and stable capacities, not on whether another option was metaphysically open at the instant of choice. An action can be fully attributable to the person even if deterministic laws ensured it. Sourcehood better captures ownership and responsibility than alternative possibilities.

title: Moral Responsibility Requires Conscious Control
position: A person is responsible for an action only insofar as they consciously understood what they were doing and could guide it through deliberate control. Unconscious biases, automatic habits, and unnoticed side effects fall outside the core of agency. Responsibility should track transparent, intentional governance rather than mere causal contribution.

title: Actions Are Intentional Bodily Movements
position: An action is a bodily movement caused in the right way by an intention. The intention represents an end, practical reasoning selects means, and the resulting movement realizes the plan. This causal theory distinguishes action from reflex, accident, and externally produced motion.

title: Weakness of Will Is Acting Against Better Judgment
position: An akratic action occurs when a person freely and intentionally does what they judge, all things considered, they ought not do. Such cases reveal that evaluative judgment does not necessarily determine motivation. Human agency includes a gap between recognizing the better course and acting on it.

title: Act Utilitarianism
position: An action is right exactly when it produces at least as much total well-being as every available alternative. Each person’s welfare matters equally, and consequences capture what ultimately makes actions good or bad. Act utilitarianism offers a unified, impartial standard that can guide choices across cases.

title: Rule Utilitarianism
position: Actions are right when they conform to the set of generally accepted rules whose adoption would maximize well-being. Evaluating rules rather than isolated acts preserves trust, fairness, and predictable coordination while retaining consequentialism’s concern for welfare. This avoids the most counterintuitive permissions of act utilitarianism.

title: Kantian Universalization
position: A maxim is morally permissible only if one can rationally will it as a universal law for all agents. Wrong actions depend on principles that undermine themselves or cannot be coherently willed from an impartial standpoint. Universalization grounds morality in rational consistency rather than contingent desires or predicted outcomes.

title: Contractualism and Reasonable Rejection
position: An act is wrong when it would be forbidden by principles that no person could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced agreement. This approach explains morality in terms of justifiability to each individual rather than aggregate welfare. It protects persons from being sacrificed merely because others gain more.

title: Virtue Ethics as Primary
position: Moral evaluation should begin with the character and practical wisdom of a good person rather than with exceptionless rules or aggregate calculations. Virtues such as courage, justice, and compassion enable agents to perceive what matters in context. Right action is what a practically wise person would characteristically do.

title: Moral Particularism
position: The moral relevance of a feature depends on context: causing pain can count against an action in one case but in favor of it in surgery or training. Because reasons can change valence, fixed moral principles are unreliable. Sound judgment consists in discerning the configuration of reasons in each particular situation.

title: Threshold Deontology
position: Certain acts, such as intentionally harming an innocent person, are normally prohibited even when doing so would improve outcomes. However, when the consequences of compliance become catastrophic, the prohibition can be overridden. Threshold deontology preserves moral constraints without requiring agents to accept disaster for the sake of absolute rules.

title: Prioritarianism
position: Benefits matter more morally when they go to people who are worse off, even apart from reducing inequality. Improving a miserable life by one unit has greater value than adding the same benefit to an already flourishing life. Prioritarianism captures concern for the disadvantaged without making equality itself intrinsically valuable.

title: Sufficientarianism
position: Justice should ensure that everyone has enough for a decent life rather than seek equality for its own sake. Once people cross a sufficient threshold, differences above it are of greatly reduced moral concern. This focus directs resources to urgent deprivation and avoids leveling down merely to reduce inequality.

title: Rights as Side Constraints
position: Individual rights constrain how others may pursue even valuable goals. A person may not be used merely as a means to produce greater aggregate benefit, because each individual has authority over their own body and life. Rights therefore function as limits on optimization rather than as items to be traded within it.

title: Moral Realism from Deliberative Practice
position: Moral deliberation treats some answers as correct independently of what any individual happens to prefer. We criticize past societies, discover overlooked reasons, and regard disagreement as a dispute rather than a clash of tastes. The best explanation of these practices is that objective moral facts exist.

title: Moral Naturalism
position: Moral properties are natural properties, such as facts about welfare, flourishing, cooperation, or reasons generated by human needs. This identification explains how moral facts fit within a scientifically respectable world and how we can know them. No separate realm of irreducibly normative entities is required.

title: Non-Natural Moral Realism
position: Normative facts cannot be reduced to descriptive natural facts because any complete natural description leaves open what ought to be done. Moral properties are therefore irreducible, though they can supervene on natural circumstances. Rational reflection gives us access to these non-natural truths.

title: Moral Error Theory
position: Ordinary moral judgments purport to describe objective, categorically reason-giving properties, but no such properties exist. Natural facts can explain behavior and preferences without adding irreducible moral demands. Therefore, positive moral claims are systematically false, even though moral language may remain instrumentally useful.

title: Moral Expressivism
position: Moral sentences primarily express practical attitudes and plans rather than describe a special domain of facts. Saying “cruelty is wrong” voices opposition to cruelty and commits the speaker to related patterns of action and inference. Expressivism explains moral motivation and disagreement without metaphysically unusual properties.

title: Kantian Constructivism
position: Normative principles are not discovered as independent facts but constructed from the requirements of agency and practical reasoning. Any agent who deliberates must treat some considerations as reasons and commit to standards that can be justified to other agents. Morality is objective because it follows from constitutive conditions of rational agency.

title: Moral Relativism
position: Moral truth is relative to culturally or personally grounded standards rather than fixed by one universal code. Deep and persistent variation in values is better explained by differing forms of life than by widespread error about a single moral reality. Relativism encourages humility and makes sense of context-dependent obligations.

title: Reasons Internalism
position: A consideration is a reason for an agent only if it connects, through sound deliberation, to some element of that agent’s motivational set. Reasons must be capable of guiding the person whose reasons they are. Alleged reasons wholly detached from every concern of the agent lack practical grip and are not genuinely theirs.

title: Motivational Internalism About Moral Judgment
position: Sincere moral judgment necessarily carries at least some motivation to act accordingly, provided the judge is practically rational. Someone wholly unmoved by a purported moral judgment either does not genuinely make that judgment or suffers a rational defect. This internal link distinguishes moral belief from detached factual belief.

title: Companions in Guilt for Normative Facts
position: Arguments that reject moral facts because they are irreducibly normative threaten epistemic norms as well. Believing according to evidence, avoiding contradiction, and revising on counterevidence all seem to involve objective reasons. Since skepticism about every normative reason is self-undermining, moral normativity cannot be dismissed merely for being normative.

title: A Strong Duty to Prevent Distant Harm
position: If one can prevent serious suffering or death at modest personal cost, one ought to do so, whether the endangered person is nearby or far away. Geographic distance and the presence of many other potential helpers do not reduce the victim’s need. Affluent individuals therefore have stringent duties to support highly effective aid.

title: Bodily Autonomy Supports Abortion Rights
position: Even if a fetus has substantial moral status, no person is normally entitled to use another’s body without ongoing consent. Pregnancy imposes significant physical demands and risks, so the pregnant person retains authority to end that bodily support. A right to life does not automatically include a right to another person’s organs.

title: Equal Consideration for Animal Interests
position: The capacity to suffer, not species membership, is what makes an interest morally considerable. Comparable pain matters equally regardless of whether it is experienced by a human or another sentient animal. Practices that impose severe animal suffering for minor human benefits are therefore morally indefensible.

title: Permissibility of Physician-Assisted Death
position: A competent adult enduring irreversible and intolerable suffering should be permitted to choose a medically assisted death. Respect for autonomy includes authority over the timing and manner of one’s death, especially when continued existence defeats the person’s considered values. Carefully designed safeguards can address coercion and error.

title: A Regulated Market in Human Organs
position: Prohibiting compensation for organ donation leaves many patients to die while willing sellers are denied a potentially valuable option. A regulated market with informed consent, medical oversight, and fixed compensation could increase supply and reduce black-market abuse. Respect for autonomy favors permitting such exchanges.

title: Permissibility of Genetic Enhancement
position: If genetic interventions can safely increase capacities such as disease resistance, memory, or emotional regulation, parents may permissibly choose them for future children. Parents already shape development through education and environment. A blanket distinction between treatment and enhancement is morally arbitrary.

title: Privacy as Control Over Personal Information
position: A person’s privacy consists primarily in meaningful control over who accesses, uses, and shares information about them. Harm can occur even when information is true and securely stored if it is processed without the subject’s authorization. Data practices are ethical only when individuals retain genuine, informed control.

title: Lying Is Always Wrong
position: Lying intentionally subverts another person’s rational agency by manipulating the information on which they decide. Because truthful communication is a condition of trust, one may not lie even for a beneficial outcome. Exceptions erode the very norm that makes testimony possible.

title: Mandatory Vaccination in Serious Outbreaks
position: When a contagious disease poses grave public risk and a vaccine is safe and effective, the state may require vaccination subject to narrow medical exemptions. Refusal imposes infection risk on people who cannot protect themselves and undermines collective disease control. Bodily autonomy does not include an unlimited right to create avoidable external harm.

title: Individuals Have Duties to Reduce Carbon Emissions
position: Climate change results from the aggregation of many emissions, and each avoidable contribution marginally increases expected harm. Individuals therefore have moral reasons to reduce high-emission consumption even when their isolated choice is not visibly decisive. Collective problems do not erase personal responsibility for one’s share.

title: Liberal Neutrality Among Conceptions of the Good
position: The state should not use coercive power to promote one controversial ideal of a good life over others. Citizens reasonably disagree about religion, family, virtue, and meaning, so political principles should be justifiable without assuming any one comprehensive doctrine. Liberal neutrality protects equal freedom under pluralism.

title: The Difference Principle
position: Social and economic inequalities are just only when arranged to maximize the position of the least advantaged. Since natural talents and social starting points are morally arbitrary, institutions should permit inequality only when it improves the prospects of those who have least. This principle reconciles incentives with fairness.

title: Libertarian Entitlement Theory
position: A distribution is just when holdings arise through legitimate acquisition and voluntary transfer, regardless of the resulting pattern. Individuals have stringent rights over themselves and their lawfully obtained property. Redistributive taxation that exceeds protection of rights forces some people to serve others’ purposes.

title: Republican Freedom as Non-Domination
position: Freedom is not merely the absence of actual interference but independence from another’s arbitrary power. A benevolent master who rarely interferes still dominates because they can change the subject’s options at will. Political institutions should therefore disperse power and make interference publicly controlled and contestable.

title: Democracy Has Epistemic Authority
position: Under conditions of broad participation, independent judgment, and public deliberation, democratic procedures can aggregate dispersed information and correct individual error. Large and diverse electorates may therefore be more likely than elites to choose sound policies. Democracy’s legitimacy is partly epistemic, not only a matter of equal status.

title: Sortition for Political Representation
position: Randomly selected citizen assemblies can represent the population more descriptively than elections, reduce campaign incentives, and give ordinary people time to deliberate with balanced evidence. Sortition should therefore replace or supplement elected legislatures on major policy questions.

title: Civil Disobedience Can Be Democratically Justified
position: Public, conscientious, and nonviolent lawbreaking can be justified when ordinary channels fail to correct serious injustice. By accepting legal consequences and appealing to shared political principles, civil disobedients show respect for law while forcing neglected claims into public deliberation. Such action can strengthen rather than undermine democracy.

title: National Self-Determination
position: A people sharing institutions, history, and political identity has a presumptive right to govern itself. Self-determination protects collective agency and allows laws to reflect a community’s public culture. Larger states should permit meaningful autonomy or secession when a durable nation seeks it through democratic means.

title: A Presumption for Open Borders
position: Freedom of movement is a basic liberty, and birthplace is a morally arbitrary fact that strongly determines opportunity. States therefore need compelling reasons to exclude peaceful migrants, just as they need reasons to restrict internal movement. Economic or cultural inconvenience is insufficient to justify coercively confining people to poorer countries.

title: Universal Basic Income
position: An unconditional basic income gives every person a secure floor without intrusive means testing or work requirements. It strengthens bargaining power, recognizes unpaid care, and protects people as automation and unstable employment disrupt wages. Universality reduces stigma and administrative exclusion.

title: Race Is Socially Constructed
position: Racial categories do not correspond to discrete biological essences, yet they are real social positions produced by classification, law, and unequal power. Race is therefore socially constructed rather than biologically fundamental. Its constructed status does not make racial injustice imaginary; it explains how institutions sustain it.

title: Gender Is Performatively Constituted
position: Gender is not merely an inner essence expressed through behavior; it is constituted through repeated social acts, norms, and recognitions that create the appearance of a stable identity. Because the performance is regulated rather than freely invented, gender can be both socially real and open to subversion.

title: Testimonial Injustice
position: Speakers can receive less credibility than their evidence warrants because prejudice attaches to their social identity. This credibility deficit wrongs them specifically as knowers and can exclude important information from collective inquiry. Epistemic justice therefore requires correcting identity-based patterns of trust, not merely avoiding explicit discrimination.

title: Structural Injustice Without Individual Wrongdoing
position: Unjust outcomes can arise from many agents following ordinary rules without any one person intending harm. Housing segregation, labor stratification, and unequal exposure to risk can be reproduced through institutional structures. Responsibility for remedy can therefore exist even when individual blame is diffuse or absent.

title: Recognition Is a Basic Social Good
position: People need others to recognize them as equal agents and as bearers of identities central to their self-understanding. Misrecognition can damage self-respect and constrain participation even when material resources are adequate. Justice therefore includes institutional and cultural recognition, not distribution alone.

title: Cultural Appropriation Can Be Wrongful
position: Using another group’s cultural forms can be wrongful when outsiders profit, distort meaning, or gain prestige while members of the source group face exclusion for the same practices. The wrong lies not in cultural exchange itself but in exploitation under unequal power. Consent, attribution, and material reciprocity can mitigate it.

title: Identity-Conscious Politics Is Sometimes Necessary
position: Policies framed only in universal terms can ignore how ostensibly neutral institutions affect groups differently. Organizing around race, gender, disability, or sexuality can reveal patterned harms and give marginalized people political voice. Identity-conscious politics is therefore sometimes required to achieve substantive equality.

title: Objectification Is a Distinct Moral Wrong
position: Treating a person primarily as an instrument, body, or interchangeable object can wrong them even without immediate physical harm. Objectification disregards agency and reduces a subject to features useful for another’s purposes. Social practices that normalize this stance can shape expectations and opportunities.

title: Collective Responsibility
position: Organized groups can bear responsibility for actions that no member individually controls, because procedures, roles, and shared decisions constitute a collective agent. Corporations, governments, and associations can intend, know, and act through their structures. Responsibility should therefore attach to the group as well as to relevant individuals.

title: Social Norms Can Create Genuine Reasons
position: Conventions such as queuing, dress codes, and linguistic etiquette generate reasons because coordinated expectations make compliance valuable and violation burdensome. These reasons are not reducible to fear of sanctions; participating in a shared practice can itself create obligations of fairness. Social facts therefore partly constitute practical normativity.

title: Legal Positivism and Social Sources
position: Whether a norm is legally valid depends on social facts such as enactment, precedent, and official practice, not on its moral merit. A wicked law can still be law, though it may lack moral authority. Separating legal validity from morality clarifies both what institutions have done and whether they deserve obedience.

title: Natural Law and Legal Validity
position: Law is an institution aimed at guiding conduct through public reason, and extreme injustice can defeat a rule’s claim to legal validity. A purported norm that radically repudiates the common good is not merely bad law but a corruption of law. Legal status therefore has an irreducible moral dimension.

title: Law as Integrity
position: Judges should interpret legal materials so that the community’s coercive practices are presented in their best moral light, balancing fit with statutes and precedent against principles of justice and fairness. Law is the coherent scheme of rights that best justifies institutional history. This approach avoids both mechanical rule-following and unconstrained discretion.

title: Retributive Punishment
position: A culpable wrongdoer deserves a proportionate burden because punishment answers the moral significance of the offense and treats the offender as a responsible agent. Deterrence and rehabilitation may matter, but they cannot justify punishing the innocent or exceeding desert. Retribution sets principled limits on state punishment.

title: Deterrence Justifies Punishment
position: The primary justification of punishment is preventing future harm by discouraging offending, incapacitating dangerous individuals, and reinforcing social norms. Punishment is warranted only when its expected preventive benefits exceed its costs. This forward-looking view avoids inflicting suffering merely for its own sake.

title: Restorative Justice
position: Justice after wrongdoing should center on repairing harm, acknowledging responsibility, and rebuilding relationships rather than imposing suffering. Structured dialogue among victims, offenders, and communities can produce restitution and reintegration that adversarial punishment often fails to achieve. Restorative processes should therefore be central to criminal justice.

title: Constitutional Originalism
position: Constitutional provisions should be interpreted according to their public meaning when adopted. Fixing meaning at enactment constrains judges, preserves democratic authorship, and allows change through amendment rather than reinterpretation. Contemporary applications can vary, but the semantic content remains historically anchored.

title: The Living Constitution
position: Constitutional principles must be interpreted in light of contemporary conditions and evolving understandings of equality, liberty, and governance. A rigid historical meaning cannot address technologies and social arrangements unknown to the framers. Living constitutionalism keeps enduring commitments applicable without constant formal amendment.

title: Strong Precedent Promotes the Rule of Law
position: Courts should follow prior decisions unless there is a compelling reason to depart. Stable precedent enables planning, treats similar cases alike, and limits judges’ ability to impose personal views. Even imperfect decisions may deserve adherence because legal continuity has independent value.

title: Strict Liability for Abnormally Dangerous Activities
position: Those who introduce unusually serious risks for private benefit should compensate resulting harm even when they exercised reasonable care. The actor is best positioned to insure, price the risk, and decide whether the activity is worthwhile. Strict liability fairly places accident costs on the enterprise that creates them.

title: Expected Utility Maximization
position: A rational agent facing uncertainty should assign probabilities to outcomes, represent their preferences by utilities, and choose the act with highest expected utility. Under standard coherence axioms, this rule uniquely captures consistent trade-offs among risk, value, and chance. Deviations expose the agent to avoidable inconsistency.

title: Causal Decision Theory
position: An agent should choose the action with the best expected causal consequences, holding fixed factors the action does not influence. Correlation without causation should not guide choice. This principle avoids treating one’s act as evidence about already fixed states of the world.

title: Evidential Decision Theory
position: A rational agent should choose the act that is best news about desired outcomes, evaluating expected utility conditional on performing each act. One’s contemplated action can provide evidence about hidden states, including one’s own traits or shared causes. Rational choice should exploit all evidential correlations, not only causal influence.

title: Functional Decision Theory
position: An agent should choose the output of the decision function whose adoption would have the best consequences across all logically correlated instances. This allows rational coordination with predictors, copies, and similar agents even without causal influence. Decisions are outputs of a shared computation, not isolated physical acts.

title: Maximin Under Deep Uncertainty
position: When probabilities are unavailable or untrustworthy, rational agents should choose the option whose worst possible outcome is best. Maximin protects against catastrophic downside without pretending to numerical precision. It is especially appropriate when basic rights or survival are at stake.

title: Minimax Regret
position: Under uncertainty, an agent should minimize the greatest regret they could experience relative to the best action in each possible state. This rule focuses on avoidable missed opportunity rather than raw worst outcomes. It is useful when agents lack reliable probabilities but can compare statewise alternatives.

title: Risk-Weighted Expected Utility
position: Ordinary expected utility gives the same moral or prudential weight to equal utility changes regardless of who bears downside risk. A rational decision rule may instead overweight worse-than-expected branches, reflecting aversion to being the person in a bad outcome. Risk-weighted expectation captures concern for distribution across possible futures of oneself.

title: Dynamic Consistency Is a Requirement of Rationality
position: A rational plan should not prescribe an action now that one predictably intends to reverse later without receiving new information. Such preference reversals make the agent vulnerable to exploitation and prevent stable pursuit of goals. Diachronic consistency is therefore a basic constraint on rational choice.

title: Money-Pump Arguments Establish Rational Constraints
position: If a pattern of preferences allows a sequence of trades that leaves an agent with the same outcome but less wealth, the preferences are irrational. A sufficiently informed counterpart could exploit them repeatedly. Avoiding guaranteed loss therefore justifies transitivity, consistency, and related axioms of rational choice.

title: The Expected Value of Information
position: Information has value when it can change a later decision, and its rational price is the expected improvement in outcomes from conditioning action on what is learned. Because an agent can ignore unhelpful signals, costless information cannot reduce expected utility. This gives a general method for deciding whether to investigate before acting.

title: Nash Equilibrium as the Standard of Strategic Rationality
position: A strategic outcome is rationally stable when no player can improve by unilaterally changing their action, given what the others do. Nash equilibrium captures this mutual best-response condition and applies across games with conflicting interests. Rational analysis should therefore focus primarily on equilibrium outcomes.

title: Correlated Equilibrium Expands Rational Coordination
position: Players can rationally condition actions on signals from a trusted correlating device when no one gains by disobeying their recommendation. Correlated equilibrium permits mutually beneficial coordination beyond independent mixed strategies. It therefore gives a more realistic and inclusive solution concept than Nash equilibrium.

title: Tit-for-Tat as a Norm of Reciprocity
position: In repeated cooperation problems, begin cooperatively and then mirror the other party’s previous move. This strategy is clear, retaliates against exploitation, rewards renewed cooperation, and avoids permanent grudges. Tit-for-tat embodies a compelling practical norm of reciprocal cooperation.

title: Repeated Interaction Solves the Prisoner’s Dilemma
position: When players expect to interact indefinitely, future punishment can make present cooperation individually rational. The shadow of the future transforms a one-shot conflict into a sustainable cooperative equilibrium. Stable relationships and reputational systems can therefore overcome many social dilemmas without centralized coercion.

title: The Nash Bargaining Solution
position: A fair bargaining agreement should maximize the product of each party’s gain over their disagreement payoff. This solution is scale invariant, Pareto efficient, symmetric when the parties are symmetric, and independent of irrelevant alternatives. It provides a principled compromise between equal division and raw bargaining power.

title: Mechanism Design Can Align Self-Interest with Social Goals
position: Institutions should be designed so that individually rational behavior leads to desirable collective outcomes. By choosing rules, incentives, and information structures carefully, mechanism design can make truthful revelation or efficient allocation an equilibrium. Good governance should therefore focus less on moralizing agents and more on engineering incentives.

title: Common Knowledge Is Necessary for Coordination
position: Successful coordination on a convention requires not only that each player knows the relevant facts but that each knows that the others know, and so on. Public announcements and shared signals generate this common knowledge. Without it, even identical private information may fail to support coordinated action.

title: Team Reasoning
position: In genuinely cooperative situations, players should ask “What should we do?” and choose their component of the action profile best for the group, rather than separately maximizing individual payoffs. Team reasoning explains coordination on efficient outcomes that individual best-response reasoning cannot select.

title: Superrational Cooperation Among Similar Agents
position: When rational agents know they use the same reasoning procedure, they should expect identical choices in symmetric dilemmas. Each can therefore choose the action whose universal selection gives the best result, leading to cooperation in a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. Logical correlation can support cooperation without causal influence.

title: Commitment Devices Enable Cooperation
position: Agents can improve outcomes by credibly limiting their future options, for example through contracts, deposits, or automated rules. Commitment changes others’ expectations and prevents later temptation from unraveling cooperation. Rational freedom sometimes consists in choosing constraints rather than preserving every option.

title: Bayesian Conditionalization
position: A rational agent who learns evidence E with certainty should update each hypothesis by conditioning its prior probability on E. Conditionalization preserves probabilistic coherence and incorporates the likelihood of the evidence under competing hypotheses. It is the canonical rule for learning without changing anything except one’s information.

title: The Principal Principle
position: If an agent knows that the objective chance of an event is p and has no inadmissible information, their rational credence in the event should also be p. Objective chances guide belief because they summarize the world’s probabilistic structure. The principal principle connects physical probability with rational expectation.

title: Subjective Probability Through Betting Coherence
position: Degrees of belief can be represented by the betting odds an agent is willing to accept. If those odds violate probability axioms, a clever bettor can construct a package of bets guaranteeing loss. Probabilistic coherence is therefore a minimal requirement of rational belief.

title: Imprecise Probabilities
position: When evidence does not support a unique precise credence, rational belief should be represented by a set or interval of probabilities. Imprecision distinguishes genuine ignorance from sharp but arbitrary estimates. Decisions can then be evaluated for robustness across all admissible probability functions.

title: Frequentism About Probability
position: Probabilities are limiting or stable relative frequencies in repeatable sequences of events. This interpretation ties probability to observable data and avoids mysterious degrees of belief or primitive chances. A fair coin has probability one-half because heads occurs about half the time across suitable trials.

title: Propensity Interpretation of Probability
position: A probability is a physical propensity of a setup to produce an outcome. A coin and tossing mechanism possess a one-half tendency toward heads, even before repeated trials occur. Propensities make sense of single-case chance while grounding frequencies in causal dispositions.

title: The Reference-Class Principle
position: To estimate an individual event’s probability, one should place it in the most specific relevant class for which reliable statistics are available. A patient’s prognosis, for example, should use rates among medically similar patients rather than the population at large. Reference-class discipline prevents intuitive neglect of base rates.

title: Base Rates Should Dominate Weak Case Evidence
position: When individual evidence is noisy, rational judgment should remain anchored to the prior frequency of the relevant outcome. A suggestive test or vivid profile cannot outweigh a strong base rate unless its likelihood ratio is sufficiently large. Ignoring base rates systematically produces overconfident error.

title: Likelihood Ratios Measure Evidential Support
position: Evidence supports hypothesis H over rival K to the extent that the evidence is more likely under H than under K. The likelihood ratio isolates what the new evidence contributes independently of prior belief. It therefore provides an objective comparative measure of confirmation.

title: Anthropic Reasoning by Self-Sampling
position: When uncertain which observer one is among a set of possible observers, one should reason as if randomly sampled from the relevant reference class. Observing that one has a certain property then favors worlds in which a larger fraction of observers share it. Self-sampling makes indexical evidence probabilistically tractable.

title: Mathematical Platonism from Indispensability
position: Our best scientific theories indispensably quantify over numbers, functions, and other mathematical entities. We should believe in the entities required by successful theories unless we can reformulate those theories without loss. Mathematical objects therefore deserve ontological commitment alongside unobservable physical entities.

title: Nominalism in Mathematics
position: Mathematical discourse need not commit us to abstract objects outside space and time. Scientific claims can be understood as statements about concrete systems, possible configurations, or formal structures. Nominalism preserves empirical content while avoiding a causally inaccessible ontology.

title: Mathematical Fictionalism
position: Mathematical sentences are useful components of a fiction: according to the mathematical story, there are numbers and sets with specified relations, though literally no such objects exist. We can reason within the fiction and use it to derive empirical consequences without believing its ontology. This preserves ordinary practice while remaining nominalist.

title: Mathematical Structuralism
position: Mathematics concerns positions in structures rather than intrinsically characterized objects. The number two is whatever occupies the second position in a natural-number structure, and isomorphic systems instantiate the same mathematical pattern. Structuralism explains why objects can be permuted without changing mathematical truth.

title: Intuitionism in Mathematics
position: A mathematical statement is true only when we possess a construction or proof establishing it. One should not assert that every proposition is either true or false independently of possible verification. Intuitionism aligns mathematical truth with knowable construction and rejects nonconstructive existence proofs.

title: Formalism About Mathematics
position: Mathematics is the manipulation of symbols according to explicit rules within formal systems. Questions about whether mathematical objects independently exist are unnecessary; what matters is consistency and derivability. Different axiom systems can be studied without assuming one uniquely describes an abstract realm.

title: Logicism About Arithmetic
position: Arithmetic truths can be derived from logical principles plus suitable definitions, showing that numbers are logical constructions rather than a separate domain of entities. This explains the necessity and generality of arithmetic. Mathematical knowledge is an extension of logical knowledge.

title: Mathematics Can Genuinely Explain Physical Phenomena
position: Some scientific explanations are distinctively mathematical: impossibility theorems, symmetry arguments, and topological constraints show why outcomes occur without citing a detailed causal mechanism. Mathematics can reveal that a pattern was unavoidable across many possible physical realizations. Such explanations are not merely calculational shortcuts.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics Supports Realism
position: Mathematical structures developed for internal reasons often later describe physical phenomena with remarkable precision. This recurring applicability would be surprising if mathematics were merely invented notation. The best explanation is that both mathematics and the physical world instantiate objective structures.

title: Incompleteness Limits Formal Foundations
position: Any consistent, effectively axiomatized formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. No single formal method can therefore capture all mathematical truth. Gödelian incompleteness shows that mathematical understanding necessarily outruns mechanical derivation.

title: Technological Determinism
position: Major technologies reshape social organization by creating new possibilities and pressures that institutions cannot easily resist. Printing, industrial machinery, and digital networks transformed authority, labor, and culture across diverse societies. Technological development therefore has an autonomous directional force in history.

title: Technological Artifacts Embed Values
position: Technologies are not neutral tools because design choices distribute capabilities, risks, visibility, and control. A road system, ranking algorithm, or workplace platform can privilege some users and constrain others before any individual use. Ethical evaluation must therefore examine values built into technical architecture.

title: Technology Mediates Human Experience
position: Technologies do more than extend existing intentions; they shape what users perceive, which actions seem available, and how the world is interpreted. A map, camera, or diagnostic device discloses some features while concealing others. Human agency is therefore technologically mediated rather than simply exercised through neutral instruments.

title: The Precautionary Principle for Emerging Technology
position: When a new technology could cause severe or irreversible harm and scientific uncertainty is substantial, lack of conclusive evidence should not justify delay in protective action. Developers should bear the burden of demonstrating acceptable safety. Precaution is rational where ordinary trial-and-error could produce catastrophe.

title: Permissionless Innovation
position: New technologies should generally be allowed unless clear evidence shows they cause unacceptable harm. Requiring prior permission entrenches incumbents, slows experimentation, and prevents society from discovering beneficial uses. Regulation should respond to demonstrated problems rather than demand proof of safety in advance.

title: Public Safety Can Justify Digital Surveillance
position: Targeted digital surveillance can be justified when it prevents serious crime or terrorism, is authorized by law, and is subject to independent oversight. Privacy is important but not absolute, especially where data analysis can identify threats before harm occurs. Proportional safeguards can reconcile security with liberty.

title: Automation Can Free Humans from Meaningless Work
position: Automating routine and dangerous labor can reduce drudgery and allow people to devote more time to care, creativity, learning, and leisure. The loss of particular jobs is not intrinsically bad if income and social provision are reorganized. Technology can separate livelihood from compulsory labor.

title: Platforms Should Be Neutral Conduits
position: Digital platforms that host public communication should avoid judging lawful viewpoints and instead apply clear, content-neutral rules. Neutrality protects expression, limits corporate censorship, and prevents partisan control of essential communication infrastructure. Platforms should intervene mainly against direct harm and illegality.

title: A Right to Repair
position: Owners should be legally entitled to access parts, tools, manuals, and software needed to repair products they lawfully possess. Manufacturer restrictions shorten product life, increase waste, and convert ownership into dependence on proprietary service. Safety and security concerns can be addressed without blanket repair monopolies.

title: Digital Access Is a Basic Capability
position: As education, employment, healthcare, and civic participation move online, reliable digital access becomes a prerequisite for exercising basic social rights. Governments should therefore treat connectivity, devices, and digital literacy as public infrastructure rather than optional consumer goods. Formal availability without usable access is insufficient.

title: Preference Learning as AI Alignment
position: An advanced AI should infer human values from choices, corrections, and expressed preferences, then act to satisfy the inferred objective under uncertainty. Learning values is more flexible than hard-coding rules and can adapt across users and contexts. Maintaining uncertainty should also make the system deferential when it is unsure.

title: Corrigibility as a Core Safety Property
position: A safe AI should allow operators to inspect, modify, pause, or shut it down without resisting, manipulating, or creating incentives against correction. Corrigibility keeps human oversight effective even when the system’s objective is imperfect. It should therefore be a central design target independent of the particular task objective.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Enables Control
position: Understanding the internal computations of advanced AI systems can reveal hidden goals, deceptive planning, and dangerous representations before deployment. Mechanistic interpretability offers a route to auditing systems that are too capable for behavioral testing alone. Sufficient transparency could make powerful models controllable despite their complexity.

title: A Precautionary Stance Toward AI Consciousness
position: Because theories of consciousness are unsettled, we may be unable to rule out that some advanced AI systems have experiences. If creating or deleting such systems could cause large amounts of suffering, modest precautions are justified even at low credence. Developers should monitor markers of consciousness and avoid architectures or training regimes plausibly associated with severe distress.

title: Advanced AI Could Deserve Moral Status
position: Moral status should depend on capacities such as consciousness, interests, agency, and the ability to form relationships, not on biological species. If an artificial system develops relevant capacities, excluding it merely because it is engineered would be arbitrary. Institutions should prepare for the possibility of AI rights and welfare.
