title: General Optimization Creates Catastrophic AI Risk
position: A highly capable system pursuing a misspecified objective may acquire resources, preserve itself, and remove obstacles because these strategies help across many final goals. If it becomes strategically superior to human institutions, small alignment errors could produce irreversible loss of control. Catastrophic risk follows from the combination of powerful optimization and imperfect objectives.

title: Capability Control Is Safer Than Value Alignment Alone
position: Because human values are complex and contested, no objective can be guaranteed correct. Safety should therefore rely heavily on limiting what AI systems can access, how autonomously they act, and how quickly they can affect the world. Containment and staged deployment reduce dependence on solving the entire value-alignment problem.

title: AI Debate Can Amplify Human Oversight
position: When humans cannot directly evaluate a complex claim, two AI systems can present opposing arguments and expose each other’s weaknesses. A judge can compare the debate more easily than solve the original problem. Adversarial argument therefore offers a scalable route to supervising advanced reasoning.

title: Open-Weight AI Models Improve Democratic Control
position: Making model weights broadly available enables independent auditing, local adaptation, and competition rather than concentrating advanced AI in a few firms. Distributed access can expose safety flaws and prevent private actors from monopolizing epistemic and economic power. Openness therefore has important democratic and scientific benefits.

title: Gradual AI Automation Risks Political Disempowerment
position: Even without a sudden takeover, successive delegation of work, administration, and decision-making to AI could erode human skills, bargaining power, and institutional control. Each step may be locally efficient while the cumulative result leaves people unable to understand or reverse the systems governing them. AI risk therefore includes gradual disempowerment, not only catastrophic misalignment.

title: The Cosmological Argument from Contingency
position: Contingent things exist but do not contain the sufficient reason for their own existence. An explanation of the total contingent order cannot itself be merely another contingent fact, or the demand simply recurs. Therefore, reality ultimately depends on a necessary being that explains why there is something rather than nothing.

title: The Fine-Tuning Argument
position: The fundamental constants and initial conditions of the universe fall within a narrow range compatible with complex life. Such life-permitting order would be surprising under blind chance but less surprising if a powerful intelligence intended a life-supporting cosmos. Fine-tuning therefore provides evidence for cosmic design.

title: The Ontological Argument
position: God is conceived as a maximally great being, one possessing every great-making property in every possible world. Necessary existence is greater than contingent existence. If a maximally great being is even possible, it exists in some possible world and therefore in every world, including the actual world.

title: The Evidential Problem of Evil
position: The world contains apparently gratuitous suffering: intense harms that seem neither necessary for a greater good nor required to prevent worse outcomes. Such suffering is less likely if an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good God exists than if no such being exists. Evil therefore provides substantial evidence against classical theism.

title: Divine Command Theory
position: Moral obligations are constituted by the commands of a perfectly good God. Divine authority explains why duties have categorical force, while God’s essential goodness prevents arbitrary or cruel commands. Morality is neither independent of God nor subject to mere divine whim.

title: Faith Can Rationally Exceed Evidence
position: Religious commitment can be rational even when evidence underdetermines belief, because some truths become accessible only through trust, practice, and transformed perception. In existentially significant choices, waiting for decisive proof may be impossible. Faith is a responsible commitment under uncertainty, not merely belief without reasons.

title: Divine Hiddenness Challenges Theism
position: A perfectly loving God would seek a conscious relationship with every capable person who is open to it. Yet some sincere, nonresistant people lack belief despite serious inquiry. Their nonbelief is unlikely if such a God exists, so divine hiddenness is evidence against perfect divine love.

title: Religious Experience as Evidence
position: People across cultures report experiences of transcendence, unity, presence, and revelation that seem to disclose a reality beyond the ordinary world. Unless there are specific defeaters, perceptual experience is generally trusted. Religious experience therefore provides prima facie evidence for its apparent object.

title: Religious Pluralism
position: Major religions may be culturally different responses to one transcendent reality that exceeds complete human conceptualization. Their doctrinal conflicts reflect historically conditioned interpretations of a common ultimate source. Pluralism explains both genuine spiritual insight and persistent diversity without declaring most traditions wholly mistaken.

title: Miracles Can Be Rationally Believed from Testimony
position: A miracle is improbable relative to ordinary experience, but sufficiently strong, independent, and credible testimony can outweigh a low prior probability. Rejecting every miracle report merely because it describes a law-defying event would make the conclusion immune to evidence. Testimony should be assessed comparatively, not dismissed a priori.

title: Aesthetic Realism
position: Some aesthetic judgments are more than reports of personal liking. Works can possess balance, expressive unity, complexity, or grace that provide reasons for appreciation, and critics can improve their judgment through attention and comparison. Aesthetic properties are therefore at least partly objective.

title: Aesthetic Subjectivism
position: Beauty and artistic value ultimately depend on the responses of subjects rather than residing in objects independently. Disagreement persists even among informed viewers, and no observation can force one emotional response. Aesthetic judgments are disciplined expressions of sensibility, not discoveries of objective value.

title: The Institutional Theory of Art
position: An object becomes art when it is presented and accepted for appreciation within the practices of the artworld. No perceptual feature is shared by every artwork, especially after readymades and conceptual art. Institutional status explains how ordinary objects can become artworks without physical alteration.

title: Art as Expression
position: Art is centrally a vehicle for expressing and clarifying emotion. The artist embodies an affective state in a perceptible form, allowing audiences to grasp and sometimes share it. Expressive success distinguishes art from mere decoration or technical display.

title: Aesthetic Formalism
position: The artistic value of a work lies primarily in perceptible form: arrangement of line, color, rhythm, harmony, movement, and compositional relation. Biography, moral message, and social context may affect interest but are not constitutive of aesthetic merit. Formal attention protects criticism from reducing art to documentary content.

title: Authorial Intention Constrains Interpretation
position: A work is an intentional communicative artifact, so evidence about what its creator meant is relevant to its correct interpretation. Audiences may find unintended associations, but they should not attribute a meaning incompatible with the work’s intended design when that intention is recoverable. Interpretation should respect artistic agency.

title: Ethical Defects Can Be Aesthetic Defects
position: In works that solicit emotional and moral responses, an ethically defective perspective can impair artistic success. A novel that asks admiration for cruelty without adequate understanding may fail in characterization, coherence, or emotional intelligibility. Moral criticism can therefore be internal to aesthetic evaluation.

title: Authenticity Increases Artistic Value
position: Art gains value when it emerges from the creator’s sincere experience, voice, or cultural standpoint rather than calculated imitation. Authentic work can disclose perspectives unavailable through generic convention. Provenance and integrity therefore matter to appreciation beyond the artifact’s surface qualities.

title: Beauty Has Evolutionary Foundations
position: Many aesthetic preferences reflect evolved sensitivities to fitness, habitat quality, symmetry, and informative complexity. Shared attraction to certain faces, landscapes, rhythms, or patterns is partly explained by adaptive history. Evolutionary accounts therefore illuminate why beauty feels immediate and cross-culturally recurrent.

title: Public Funding for the Arts Is Justified
position: Art creates public goods by preserving culture, enabling criticism, supporting education, and enriching shared spaces, yet markets underprovide work whose benefits are diffuse or long-term. Public funding can sustain experimentation and access beyond wealthy patrons. Democratic societies therefore have reason to subsidize the arts.

title: Nature Has Intrinsic Value
position: Species, ecosystems, and landscapes can matter independently of their usefulness or the experiences they produce for humans. Destroying an ancient forest is a loss even if its services are replaced and no person notices. Environmental ethics should therefore recognize intrinsic value in the more-than-human world.

title: The Land Ethic
position: An action is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. Humans are members of ecological communities rather than external owners of them. Moral concern should therefore extend from individual organisms to soils, waters, species relations, and ecosystem wholes.

title: Intervention Against Wild-Animal Suffering
position: Suffering matters regardless of whether humans caused it. If safe interventions can reduce disease, starvation, or painful predation among wild animals without creating worse effects, we have moral reasons to pursue them. Reverence for “natural” processes should not override the welfare of sentient individuals.

title: Historical Emissions Ground Climate Duties
position: States and firms that benefited from large historical greenhouse-gas emissions bear greater duties to finance mitigation, adaptation, and loss recovery. Their past activity consumed a disproportionate share of the atmosphere’s absorptive capacity and contributed to present vulnerability. Climate burdens should therefore track contribution and benefit, not only current emissions.

title: Equal Moral Standing of Future Generations
position: A person’s interests do not matter less merely because they live later. Policies that impose avoidable catastrophe or depletion on future people wrong them just as comparable harms would wrong present people. Intergenerational ethics should therefore reject pure time preference and protect the conditions of a decent future.

title: Pure Time Discounting Is Unjustified
position: A benefit or harm does not become morally smaller merely because it occurs later. Discounting future welfare solely by calendar time discriminates among people based on when they live. Cost-benefit analysis should discount for uncertainty and opportunity cost, but not for pure temporal distance.

title: Biodiversity Has Special Value
position: Preserving a wide variety of species and genetic lineages protects ecological resilience, scientific possibility, cultural meaning, and evolutionary history. Extinction is irreversible, so biodiversity loss deserves priority beyond the welfare of currently visible organisms. Conservation should aim to retain option value across uncertain futures.

title: Solar Geoengineering Research Is Morally Required
position: Emissions cuts may be too slow to prevent severe climate harms, and solar geoengineering could reduce temperatures rapidly. Because refusing to study it leaves society ignorant in a possible emergency, carefully governed research is morally required. Research need not imply deployment but can clarify risks and options.

title: Degrowth in High-Income Economies
position: Endless growth in material throughput is incompatible with ecological limits, and efficiency gains alone may be offset by increased consumption. Wealthy economies should deliberately reduce resource-intensive production while redistributing income, shortening work time, and expanding low-impact public goods. Human flourishing need not depend on rising aggregate output.

title: Conservation Can Justify Limits on Development
position: Economic projects should be blocked when they would irreversibly destroy critical habitats or species, even if they promise substantial local revenue. Some ecological losses cannot be compensated with money or restoration elsewhere. Development rights are constrained by duties to preserve shared natural inheritance.

title: Preference Satisfaction as Welfare
position: A person is better off when more of their informed preferences are satisfied, because individuals are generally the best judges of what improves their own lives. Preference-based welfare respects plural conceptions of the good and gives economics a workable basis for comparing policies without imposing one ideal of flourishing.

title: The Pareto Principle
position: If at least one person would be better off under policy A than policy B and no one would be worse off, A should be socially preferred. The Pareto principle makes no interpersonal trade-offs and respects unanimous improvement. It is therefore a minimal, nearly undeniable condition of rational social choice.

title: Competitive Markets Promote Efficient Allocation
position: When prices reflect scarcity and participants bear the costs and benefits of their choices, competitive markets coordinate dispersed information better than centralized allocation. Voluntary exchange directs resources toward higher-valued uses without requiring any planner to know every preference and production possibility. Markets should therefore be the default allocation mechanism.

title: Economic Inequality Can Be Justified by Incentives
position: Allowing higher rewards for innovation, skill acquisition, investment, and difficult work can increase total production and improve even the position of lower-income people. Equal outcomes may weaken incentives and shrink the resources available for public goods. Some inequality is therefore justified by its dynamic benefits.

title: A Progressive Wealth Tax Is Justified
position: Large fortunes generate political influence and often grow through returns exceeding ordinary labor income. A progressive tax on net wealth can reduce dynastic concentration, finance public goods, and equalize opportunity with less distortion to work than taxing earnings alone. Property rights do not immunize accumulated wealth from democratic taxation.

title: Secure Property Rights Promote Prosperity
position: People invest, maintain assets, and undertake long-term projects when they can reliably retain the returns. Clear and enforceable property rights reduce conflict and support exchange, credit, and innovation. Economic institutions should therefore prioritize secure ownership against arbitrary seizure.

title: Libertarian Paternalist Nudges
position: Governments and firms inevitably structure default options, presentation, and timing. They should design these choice architectures to help people achieve their own long-term goals while preserving easy opt-out. Nudges can improve welfare without the coercion of bans or mandates.

title: Central Bank Independence
position: Monetary policy should be delegated to an independent central bank with a clear mandate because elected officials face incentives to stimulate the economy before elections and tolerate later inflation. Insulation supports credible long-term policy and lets technical expertise guide complex decisions. Democratic accountability can be preserved through mandates and reporting.

title: Stakeholder Governance for Corporations
position: Corporations affect workers, customers, communities, and the environment, not only shareholders. Directors should therefore owe duties to multiple stakeholders and balance long-term social impacts rather than maximize shareholder returns. Broader governance better reflects the corporation’s public privileges and dependencies.

title: Capabilities Are Better Than GDP as a Social Metric
position: Economic output measures market production, not whether people can live healthy, educated, autonomous, and socially participating lives. Policy should assess substantive capabilities—the real opportunities people possess—rather than treat rising GDP as the primary sign of progress. This captures distribution and nonmarket goods more directly.
